title: Measuring the Output Responses to Fiscal Policy
research_question: How much does aggregate output respond to changes in government spending, and does the size of this response differ between recessions and expansions? Do the responses vary across different components of government purchases (defense vs. nondefense, consumption vs. investment), and how does accounting for the anticipated component of fiscal changes affect estimated output responses?
data_description: The analysis uses quarterly US data spanning 1947:I–2008:IV. Core macroeconomic variables include log real government purchases (federal, state, and local consumption and investment), log real net government tax receipts (direct and indirect taxes net of transfers), and log real GDP in chained 2000 dollars, with nominal series deflated by the GDP deflator. Government spending is also disaggregated into defense vs. nondefense and into consumption vs. investment components. To capture expectations, the authors collect real-time professional forecasts of output, government spending, and tax revenues from the Survey of Professional Forecasters (available for GDP from 1968 and government spending from 1982), the University of Michigan RSQE macroeconometric model (from 1982), and Federal Reserve Greenbook forecasts prepared for FOMC meetings (1966–2004). A series capturing news about future military spending from Ramey (2011) is also used. NBER recession dates serve as a benchmark for business-cycle phases.
institutional_context: The study is motivated by the post-2008 policy debate over the macroeconomic effects of fiscal stimulus in the United States, where policymakers and academics offered widely conflicting estimates of fiscal multipliers. Government economists relied on traditional large-scale macroeconometric models to evaluate stimulus packages such as the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, while critics produced contrasting predictions from alternative quantitative frameworks. A central question in this debate is whether government spending has stronger expansionary effects when the economy has slack—consistent with the Keynesian intuition that crowding out of private consumption and investment is weaker in downturns—than during expansions, when resources are more fully employed. Additional motivation comes from the recent zero-lower-bound environment, where some theoretical models suggest unusually large multipliers. The setting also reflects the heterogeneity of fiscal interventions, since stimulus packages combine defense and nondefense outlays as well as government consumption and investment, each potentially propagating differently through the economy.
